interactions.summary: Jiang says the next class will stage the battle between Virgil and Dante around love, and he draws the immediate distinction: Virgil's love contains narcissism, Dante's is unconditional.

A student brings Augustine and Christ's sacrificial suffering into the discussion, and Jiang answers that Dante asks for ego-transcendence rather than ego-erasure while stressing again that Beatrice was never a fully concrete person in his life.

Students test whether Beatrice works because death freezes her into an untouchable ideal or because her very name marks a symbolic blessed figure, and Jiang interrupts both moves, sharply resisting the reduction of her to either a child-image or a merely unreal person.

speaker_notes.note: The final 'I disagree' likely belongs to Jiang cutting off the symbolic reading, but the overlap is abrupt.

claims.claim: Jiang says it is crucial to distinguish true love because the coming Virgil-versus-Dante contrast will show narcissism in Virgil's concept of love but not in Dante's.
claims.temporal_scope: Interpretive and forward-looking claim stated on 2026-06-18 about a future class.

claims.claim: Jiang defines Dante's love as unconditional and says Dante asks people to transcend ego without abandoning it entirely.
Jiang reemphasizes that Beatrice is not a fully conceived person for Dante because their acquaintance was limited, she married someone else, and she died young in childbirth.
A student argues that Beatrice may remain perfect in Dante's mind because death freezes her image at an untouchable youthful age.
A second student suggests that Beatrice may function less as a real historical person than as a textual figure of blessedness, and Jiang immediately rejects that reduction.
claims.temporal_scope: Student interpretation and Jiang rejection stated on 2026-06-18.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang sets up the coming Virgil-versus-Dante fight as a battle over what love is, with narcissism on one side and unconditionality on the other.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there is a narcissism to his concept of love that does not exist in Dante
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a strong forward-pointing distinction likely to matter for later packets and the public read.

signature_moments.moment: Dantean love does not annihilate ego; it forces ego outward toward another person.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you have to leave your ego that you transcend your ego it doesn't mean you abandon your ego
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's clearest distinction between selfhood and self-enclosure in the packet.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The key contrast term Jiang uses to separate Dante's unconditional love from Virgil's more narcissistic conception.
Jiang's phrase for moving beyond self-enclosure without erasing the self entirely.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang explicitly flags a coming session that will contrast Virgil and Dante on love, which may sharpen or extend this packet's provisional distinction.

uncertainty_notes.note: The closing exchange is cut by interruptions and overlapping objections, so the exact final shape of Jiang's disagreement with the symbolic reading is somewhat compressed by ASR.
